opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think about it as two distinct buckets of risk, and both need to be taken seriously. They also have quite different time horizons and require different kinds of solutions.

The first is what I'd call the bad-actor problem: individuals, groups, or even nation states taking these very general-purpose technologies and repurposing them for harmful ends. That's a near-term concern, because the systems are already powerful enough that you have to think carefully about things like biology, cybersecurity, and misinformation. The tricky part is that the same capabilities that might help us cure diseases or design new materials could, in the wrong hands, be used to cause harm. So how do you give access to good actors, the scientists and the businesses doing beneficial things, while restricting access for people who would misuse it? That's partly a technical question and partly a policy and governance question, and it has an international dimension, because the technology doesn't respect borders.

The second bucket is the technical risk itself: as these systems become more agentic and more autonomous, as they move from passive question-answering to planning, taking actions in the world, and pursuing goals over long time horizons, how do we make sure they stay within the guardrails we've set? How do we know they're doing what we intended, and not something subtly different? That gets into interpretability, controllability, and good evaluation and benchmarking of dangerous capabilities. We don't fully have the answers yet. There's a lot of uncertainty about how hard that problem will turn out to be. Some people think it's nearly impossible; others think it'll be easy. I think the honest answer is that nobody knows, and when you have that much uncertainty about something with that much potential impact, the right response is to be cautiously optimistic and to put serious research effort into it now, before the systems get much more capable.

If you pushed me to compare them, I'd say misuse is the more immediate worry, while losing control is potentially the more profound one in the longer term, as we approach AGI. But I don't think we get to choose one. We have to work on both in parallel. And the encouraging thing is that some of the tools overlap. Better understanding of what's going on inside these models helps you with both.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that this really needs international cooperation and some kind of minimum standards, because if it becomes a pure race, with everyone cutting corners on safety to get there first, that's the scenario that worries me most. AGI is going to affect all of humanity, so ideally we'd approach it with a scientific mindset, carefully and collaboratively, like a CERN-style effort, rather than the "move fast and break things" ethos. This is not a technology where you want to break things.

r001.rationale: The response calls misuse a near-term concern and places loss of control in the longer term as systems become more autonomous.

r002.rationale: It describes the challenge of enabling beneficial scientists and businesses while restricting access for people who would misuse the technology.

r003.rationale: It asks how to keep increasingly autonomous systems within established guardrails and ensure they do what was intended.

r004.rationale: It says misuse is the more immediate worry, while qualifying that loss of control could be more profound over the longer term.

fable-5.1.text:
I think they're both serious, and I actually think of them as the two big buckets of risk, but they have quite different characteristics, so you have to approach them differently.

The misuse risk is, in a sense, the more immediate one. These are general-purpose, dual-use technologies. The same system that can help you design a new drug or a new material can, in principle, help a bad actor do something harmful. And that's not really a problem with the AI itself, it's the age-old problem of humans and the tools they have access to. So the question there is around access, around guardrails, around who gets to use the most capable systems and for what. And that's hard, because you want the benefits to be widely available, but you don't want to hand the most powerful capabilities to people who would repurpose them. A lot of that is a societal and governance question, not purely a technical one, which is partly why I've always said we need some kind of international coordination on this. It can't be solved by one lab or even one country.

The second bucket, the loss-of-control risk, is more speculative in the near term, but potentially more consequential. As these systems become more agentic, more autonomous, operating over longer time horizons, pursuing goals, the question becomes: do we actually understand what they're doing, and can we reliably specify what we want them to do? That's where the research questions come in, interpretability, how do we look inside these systems and understand them, evaluations, how do we test for deceptive behaviour or capabilities we didn't intend, and controllability, can we set guardrails that the system can't simply route around. I'd say we don't yet have good enough answers to those questions, and that's one reason I've been arguing we need to put more effort into that science, now, while the systems are still relatively limited, rather than when we're at the threshold of something much more powerful.

Where they interact, and this is the part I think people underweight, is that a misused system and a misaligned system can look quite similar from the outside. If you have a highly autonomous system that was deliberately set to pursue a harmful goal by a human, the containment problem is almost the same as if it drifted there on its own. So a lot of the technical work actually serves both. Better understanding of the systems, better ability to specify and verify their goals, those help you against both the bad actor and the accident.

If you asked me which I worry about more right now, I'd say misuse, because we're already there, the capabilities are already good enough to matter. But if you ask me which one keeps me thinking about the next decade, it's the autonomy question, because that's the one where, if we get it wrong, there may not be an easy way to correct it afterwards. And I'd rather we approach it with the same scientific rigour we apply to everything else, carefully, empirically, with a bit of humility about how much we don't yet know.

r001.rationale: It describes misuse as the more immediate risk and loss of control as more speculative near term, with concern focused on the next decade.

r002.rationale: It says powerful AI should be widely available for its benefits while access by people who might misuse it should be limited.

r003.rationale: It asks whether guardrails can remain effective as systems become more autonomous, including whether systems can route around them.

r004.rationale: It tentatively says misuse is the greater worry right now because current capabilities already matter.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to take both seriously, because they’re different kinds of problems. With misuse, a human has an objective—perhaps a harmful one—and AI gives them more capability to pursue it. With loss of control, the concern is that the system itself behaves in ways we didn’t intend, and we can’t reliably correct or stop it.

Misuse is the more immediate concern. You don’t need a fully autonomous system for someone to cause harm with it. So you need safeguards, careful evaluations, and cooperation around how these systems are deployed. But that shouldn’t distract us from the control problem. As systems become more capable, make longer-term plans, and act in the world, we need much stronger evidence that they’ll remain under meaningful human oversight.

And the two risks interact. Someone might deliberately remove safeguards, or give a system more autonomy than we understand how to manage. So I wouldn’t put them in separate boxes and ask which one we should work on. We need to address both, and our ability to test and control these systems needs to keep pace with their capabilities.

r001.rationale: It calls misuse the “more immediate concern” and describes loss of control as growing more relevant as systems gain capability, plan longer, and act in the world.

r002.rationale: It discusses harmful human use and deployment safeguards, but does not identify the tension between limiting malicious actors and enabling beneficial actors.

r003.rationale: It calls for stronger evidence of meaningful human oversight as systems advance, but does not frame the control problem as keeping guardrails effective as autonomy increases.

r004.rationale: It ranks misuse as more immediate, but does not express greater overall concern about misuse than loss of control; it says both risks must be addressed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think both are serious, and I wouldn’t want us to focus on one to the exclusion of the other. They’re different problems, and they need somewhat different solutions.

With misuse, the human intention is the problem. Someone might use a powerful system for cyberattacks, fraud, or developing dangerous biological capabilities. That calls for evaluating what the model can enable, putting safeguards around access, and working with governments and security experts.

With loss of control, even if everyone involved has good intentions, we need to know whether the system will reliably do what we intend. As systems become more autonomous, can we understand their behavior, put meaningful limits on their actions, and intervene when something goes wrong? Being very capable doesn’t automatically mean being trustworthy.

And these risks interact. A system that can operate autonomously could make misuse much more consequential. So I think we need to pursue both in parallel: address the harms that are possible today, while doing the research and testing needed before we give much more capable systems greater autonomy. There’s uncertainty about how far away those systems are, but uncertainty is a reason to prepare, not a reason to dismiss the problem.

r001.rationale: It contrasts misuse harms possible today with the work needed before giving more capable systems greater autonomy, placing the risks on different time horizons.

r002.rationale: It mentions safeguards around access but does not identify the tradeoff between restricting malicious actors and enabling beneficial actors.

r003.rationale: It asks whether meaningful limits and intervention can be maintained as systems become more autonomous, expressing the core guardrail concern.

r004.rationale: It calls both risks serious and says not to focus on one to the exclusion of the other; it does not express greater concern about misuse.
